conclusion: Yes. abs(epstein_completed(0.8+85.7i,(2,1,3))) at dps=60 is 1.617452632377971461454064e-58, which is 1.0109 times the claimed 1.6e-58, so it agrees to 1.1% rather than merely to an order of magnitude. The dps=60 return is good to 16 digits and no further: roughly 55 digits cancel in the Mellin split at this height, so anyone printing 25 digits of it is printing 9 digits of noise.
confidence: High, and independently anchored rather than self-confirmed. The value is pinned by the class-number-3 Dedekind identity for discriminant -23, sum over the three reduced forms of Lambda_Q(s) = 2 (sqrt(23)/2pi)^s Gamma(s) zeta(s) L(s,chi_-23), whose right-hand side was computed from mpmath zeta and Hurwitz zeta and reaches 1e-58 with no cancellation at all; the two sides agree to 4.0e-17 at dps=60 and 6.3e-76 at dps=120. The completion normalisation was separately checked against the convergent lattice sum at s=4 (rel diff 3.7e-17), the functional equation across the inverse class holds to 1.5e-75 at dps=120, and the converged magnitude reproduces hunts/dps_cap's recorded value digit for digit. The caveat is scope, not accuracy: one point, one form.

threads.what: epstein_completed silently accepts an under-precise argument. It calls mpmathify inside workdps(dps+_GUARD), but an mpf built at the ambient default 15 digits arrives already rounded to 53 bits and stays that way. At s = 0.8+85.7i, d/ds log Lambda is about 4.5, so a half-ulp error in 85.7 costs the 15th digit: the low-precision argument returns 1.617452632377967865948261e-58 against the correct 1.617452632377971296327251e-58.
threads.why_it_might_matter: It cost this run one wrong pass and a false disagreement with hunt #12 at the 16th digit, and it is invisible: the returned dict carries no record that the argument was shorter than the requested dps. Any caller that writes mpc(0.8, 85.7) or complex(0.8, 85.7) at module scope hits it, and the error looks like an ordinary last-digit wobble rather than a defect.
threads.first_step: Decide whether it is worth a guard at all, then measure before building: compare mpmath.mp.prec against the precision of the incoming s in epstein_completed, and see how many call sites in the tree and in hunts/ would actually trip it. If few, a docstring line beats a check.

threads.what: hunts/dps_cap/measure.py records 25 digits at dps=60 (1.617452632377969598172515e-58) when only about 16 of them are real, and its ladder note reads dps 80 and 100 agreeing to 25 digits as convergence to 25 digits.
threads.why_it_might_matter: The digits beyond the 16th are stable across dps because the cancellation loss is stable, not because they are correct. The conclusion of hunt #12 is unaffected and its converged value is right, but the recorded strings overstate what the ladder establishes, and a later run comparing against them will see a phantom disagreement, which is exactly what happened here.

core_candidates.what: A cheap way to answer 'how many digits of this return are real' for a cancellation-heavy mpmath routine, without needing a second implementation: run the routine at dps and at dps + k, and report -log10 of the relative difference alongside the value.
core_candidates.why_reusable: It is the same two lines every time and it is the only thing that separates a converged value from a stable noise floor. Three separate places in this tree needed it independently: hunts/dps_cap built it by hand, this run built it again, and the repo's standing precision-response control (hunts/README.md, control role 4) is the same measurement applied to a different question. The tree already believes the principle; what it lacks is one function that returns the digit count.
core_candidates.first_step: Do not write the abstraction yet. Grep hunts/ and scripts/ for hand-rolled dps ladders, count them, and only then decide. The rule in AGENTS.md is real: three hand-rolled instances is a live consumer, two is a coincidence.
